tier_reason: First-party README shows a single shell `time` run of ack, ag and pt on the Linux kernel tree, with no CPU model, tool versions, Go version or build flags, so it falls short of A and is first-party (C).

corrections.baseline: The Silver Searcher (ag, written in C: ggreer/the_silver_searcher has src/main.c) and ack (Perl); versions of all three tools not stated.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README benchmark (one run per tool, shell time, Linux kernel tree): ack 32.613 s total (30.18 s user, 2.32 s system, 99% cpu), ag 1.069 s total (1.57 s user, 1.76 s system, 311% cpu), pt 0.991 s total (2.29 s user, 1.26 s system, 358% cpu). README Features claim pt is 'about 3-5x faster than ack' and 'as fast as' ag. By wall time pt is about 1.08x (8%) faster than ag and about 33x faster than ack (derived from page data), but it uses more CPU time than ag (3.55 s vs 3.33 s, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Single run on an unspecified machine, with no tool versions, Go version, kernel tree revision or flags; the 8% wall-time gap over ag is within one-run noise, and pt spends more total CPU time than ag. The runs are listed in the order ack, ag, pt, so pt probably ran on the warmest page cache (inference; order of execution not stated). Both ag and pt are multithreaded, so the result is a tool-versus-tool comparison, not a language-level one; the README states no mechanism. Last commit 2018-09-05 (Travis CI and wercker badges). ripgrep, already in the catalog, is the common choice today.

notes: README numbers match the record exactly; ag is confirmed C. Keep at C with shortcomings: one run, no hardware or versions, wall-time win over the C baseline of only about 8% with higher CPU use, abandoned since 2018.

tier_reason: First-party BENCH.md with public harness (bench/bench.sh driven by .github/workflows/bench.yml) and the runner CPU (Xeon Platinum 8272CL), but the rustc version, the GNU wc version and build, and the locale are not recorded, so it falls short of A.

corrections.workload: bench/bench.sh, run by the workflow_dispatch job cli_bench in .github/workflows/bench.yml on ubuntu-latest (2 vCPUs): hyperfine 1.15.0 (-m 100 minimum runs, -w 2 warmups) of wz against GNU wc over the 11 files in crates/wz-utf8/tests/resources (about 3.17 MB in total, mostly world192.txt 2.41 MB and Lorem_big.txt 0.75 MB, plus small Arabic, French, Spanish and sample files and an empty file): wz -b vs wc -c, -w vs -w, wz -c vs wc -m, -l vs -l, -L vs -L, default mode, and a high-load case with the file list tripled. The script also produces max-length.md, but BENCH.md does not publish the -L table.
corrections.claimed_speedup: BENCH.md hyperfine means (wz vs wc, relative factor as printed): chars (wz -c vs wc -m) 1.9 ms vs 19.8 ms (10.46 +/- 3.16x); default mode 7.3 ms vs 21.4 ms (2.95 +/- 0.19x); words 7.5 ms vs 20.5 ms (2.72 +/- 0.32x); high load 14.9 ms vs 58.2 ms (3.90 +/- 0.29x); lines 1.8 ms vs 2.2 ms (1.20 +/- 0.10x). Bytes go the other way: wz -b 1.9 ms vs wc -c 0.8 ms (wz 2.44 +/- 0.61x slower). No max-line-length result is published.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: wz built by `cargo install --path .` with the Rust stable toolchain current at run time (version not recorded), Cargo.toml release profile: opt-level 2, fat LTO, codegen-units 1, panic abort, strip; bytecount with the runtime-dispatch-simd feature. GNU wc is the ubuntu-latest runner's coreutils binary (version, build flags and locale not recorded).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 4 stars, 0 forks; crates.io package wz, 10,947 downloads (32 recent), latest version 1.0.3 published 2022-11-04
corrections.caveats: Inputs are small (about 3.17 MB across 11 files), so runs of 2 to 60 ms include process start-up. wz counts the files in parallel with rayon on the 2-vCPU runner while wc is single-threaded. The char and word wins depend on the locale, which is not recorded: wz counts chars with bytecount::num_chars (SIMD count of non-continuation bytes) and words with an ASCII-only isspace byte fold (0x20, 0x09, 0x0A-0x0D), whereas GNU wc -m and -w in a UTF-8 locale decode every multibyte character and test Unicode whitespace, so the two tools do different work for -w and may differ on non-ASCII whitespace (inference from the sources; wc under LC_ALL=C would not decode). wz loses the plain byte count (wc -c answers from file size). The -L results were produced but not published. No commits since 2023-08-01 (dependabot bumps); 4 stars.
corrections.why_faster: From the sources (crates/wz-utf8/src/lib.rs, Cargo.toml): SIMD counting via the bytecount crate for chars (num_chars) and lines (count), memchr for line scanning in the max-length counter, an ASCII-only whitespace test for words with no multibyte decoding, and rayon parallelism across files; GNU wc in a UTF-8 locale decodes multibyte characters per character (locale unrecorded, inference). The gain comes from libraries, parallelism and a simpler word definition, not from Rust codegen.

notes: All BENCH.md numbers match the record; input files identified (crates/wz-utf8/tests/resources, about 3.17 MB). Keep at C with shortcomings: locale and wc version unrecorded, wz parallel vs single-threaded wc on 2 vCPUs, word definition is ASCII-only vs wc's locale-aware decoding, loses byte count, -L table unpublished, abandoned since 2023-08.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the benchmark code is public for both sides (languages/C/bench.c, languages/C++/bench.cpp, languages/Zig/bench.zig, run_benchmarks.sh, Nix-pinned toolchains in flake.nix/flake.lock), and the README states the compilers (GCC 16.2.0, Zig 0.16.0), the exact flags and the CPU (Ryzen 9 5900X locked at 3.5 GHz). The record's C cap ('source states no mechanism') is not a tier rule; the mechanism is now stated from the Zig standard library source. Single run per language is a caveat, not a tier criterion.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README results table (3 September 2026, one run per language), String Operations column: Zig 1.504 s, C 2.132 s, C++ 2.190 s, C# 2.235 s, D 2.351 s, Go 2.532 s, Ada 2.603 s, Rust 2.621 s, Nim 2.804 s. Zig is 1.42x faster than C and 1.46x faster than C++ (derived from page data). Zig is not faster overall: Fibonacci Zig 3.181 s vs C 1.694 s, and C ranks first on total runtime (9.762 s vs Zig 10.737 s, Zig factor 1.10x).
corrections.caveats: One run per language (the runner supports --runs 3 but the published table is a single run); the CPU is locked at 3.5 GHz and the gap is 42%, so noise alone is unlikely to explain it. The win belongs to the Zig standard library's equality routine, not to Zig codegen: std.mem.eql inlines a branch-light short-slice compare (three byte XORs below 4 bytes, four overlapping 4-byte loads up to 16 bytes) and returns early when both slices share a pointer, which skips the byte compare on the 19 diagonal pairs of each iteration; the C and C++ versions call out-of-line glibc memcmp (variable length, so GCC presumably does not inline it; disassembly not checked) for each of the 103 equal-length pairs of the 361 per iteration. A C version with an inlined compare would likely close the gap (inference). The input is a compile-time constant 19-word sentence (README says constant folding counts as a result); C tokenises a strdup copy with strtok at run time while Zig tokenises the constant slice, so LLVM may specialise more (not checked). Zig 0.16.0's lib/std/mem.zig was not readable (the tag is not on the GitHub mirror); the eqlBytes code was read at 0.15.1 and master. Rust and Go are also slower than C on this task, and C ranks first overall in the same repository.
corrections.why_faster: Library and inlining (from the sources): Zig's std.mem.eql dispatches to eqlBytes (lib/std/mem.zig, read at 0.15.1 and master), which is inlined into the loop and, for slices of at most 16 bytes, compares with three byte XORs (length below 4) or four overlapping 4-byte loads after a pointer-equality shortcut; the C side calls glibc memcmp and the C++ side std::string_view operator== (libstdc++, which also reaches memcmp) once per equal-length pair, paying an out-of-line call on 2- to 6-byte words. The gain is the Zig standard library's short-slice equality routine, not codegen, autovectorisation or the allocator.

notes: Numbers and flags match the README exactly; same algorithm and equivalent opt level (gcc/g++ -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops vs zig -OReleaseFast -mcpu=native), so tier upgraded to A on the published methodology. Record shortcomings: one run per language, a narrow microbenchmark on tiny constant strings, the win comes from Zig's std.mem.eql (inlined short compare plus pointer-equality shortcut that does slightly less work on the diagonal) against an out-of-line glibc memcmp call, and C still wins on total runtime.
